title: Good Will, Ill Will
theme: The roots bene and mal: good and bad
objectives: I can use the roots bene (good, well) and mal (bad, badly) to predict the meaning of an unfamiliar word.
I can tell apart words for ill will (malice, malicious, malevolent) by how strong and how active the harm is.
I can distinguish benign from malignant and beneficial from benevolent, and use each correctly.
I can use the endings -ent, -ous, and -ary to build and understand related words.
rationale: Bene and mal are close to perfect opposites, which makes them an ideal first Latin-root pair for grade 8: students who know that bene means good and mal means bad can decode a whole family of academic words they will meet in science, civics, and literature. The unit pairs words so that each contrast teaches the other (benevolent and malevolent, benign and malignant, benefactor and beneficiary), and adds malfunction as a word whose root is easy to see. Three of the words (benign, malice, malignant) begin with the root but hide it slightly in spelling, so the unit also practices checking a prediction against context instead of trusting a guess. Students use these words again when analyzing characters, historical figures, and the effects of rumor and misinformation.

words.def: Helpful; producing a good result or an advantage.
words.ex: Regular sleep is beneficial for memory as well as for mood.
words.ex2: The rain was beneficial to the farmers after a dry summer.
words.nonExample: Eating nothing but candy for a week is not beneficial for the body.

morph.note: The ending -ial is a spelling of -al.

apps.academic: A scientist asks whether a change in diet is beneficial for everyone or only for some groups.
apps.spoken: Talking to a coach before the tryout was beneficial.
apps.writing: Use beneficial for something that produces a good effect; choose a specific benefit to prove it.

cloze.s: Walking to school is ___ for your health, since it builds strength and clears your head before class.

cloze2.s: The new rule proved ___ to everyone: lines moved faster, and students felt less rushed.

misuse.s: Skipping sleep before an exam is beneficial because it improves memory and focus.
misuse.why: Beneficial means helpful; going without sleep hurts memory and focus.

words.def: Kind and generous, wishing to do good for other people.
words.ex: The benevolent owner let the animal shelter use the building rent-free.
words.ex2: In the fable, a benevolent king secretly paid the debts of his poorest neighbors.
words.nonExample: A leader who helps others only to be praised is not truly benevolent.

apps.academic: Historians ask whether a ruler's benevolent acts came from real concern or from a wish to be admired.
apps.spoken: She is so benevolent that she gives away half of what she earns.
apps.writing: Use benevolent for a person or action motivated by goodwill; it describes the wish to help, not just the result.

cloze.s: The ___ stranger paid for the family's groceries and asked for nothing in return.

cloze2.s: Though the teacher seemed stern, her ___ nature showed whenever a student needed extra help.

misuse.s: The benevolent landlord raised the rent again and again to push families out of the building.
misuse.why: Benevolent means wishing others well; forcing families out is the opposite.

visual.alt: Open hands holding out a wrapped gift.

words.def: A person or group that receives help, money, or an advantage from someone or something.
words.ex: The library was the main beneficiary of the charity run, receiving enough money to buy two hundred new books.
words.ex2: As the beneficiary of her aunt's will, Marcus received a small piano.
words.nonExample: A person who gives money to a charity is the donor, not the beneficiary.

morph.note: The ending -ary is spelled -iary after fic (ary becomes iary).

apps.academic: A policy's beneficiaries are the people who actually gain from it, and a fair analysis names them.
apps.spoken: Who is the beneficiary of this plan, the students or the company?
apps.writing: Use beneficiary for the person or group that gains, and name what they gain.

cloze.s: The scholarship fund's first ___ was a student who walked three miles to school every day.

cloze2.s: Each ___ of the park's garden program receives free seeds, tools, and lessons.

misuse.s: The charity's main beneficiary was the donor, who gave away the money and received nothing in return.
misuse.why: A beneficiary is the one who receives help; the donor is the one who gives it.

visual.alt: A child receiving a wrapped gift.

words.def: A person who gives money or help to a person, school, or cause.
words.ex: An anonymous benefactor paid for the new science lab.
words.ex2: The museum honored its longtime benefactor with a plaque beside the entrance.
words.nonExample: A person who takes money from a school and gives nothing back is not its benefactor.

apps.academic: Many public libraries and museums were started with gifts from a single benefactor.
apps.spoken: Our benefactor wants to stay anonymous.
apps.writing: Use benefactor for a giver whose support makes something possible; it is a person, not the gift.

cloze.s: The school's generous ___ gave enough money to repair the old gym and asked that no one use her name.

cloze2.s: Without a ___ willing to fund the trip, the orchestra could not afford tickets to the national contest.

misuse.s: The benefactor demanded payment from the school for every dollar he had supposedly given.
misuse.why: A benefactor gives help freely; demanding payment is not giving.

visual.alt: A bag of coins beside a school building.

words.frame: A benefactor made it possible for ___ to ___.

words.def: Harmless or gentle; not likely to cause damage, disease, or ill will.
words.ex: The doctor said the lump was benign and would need only a yearly checkup.
words.ex2: Her benign smile told the nervous new students that no one would laugh at them.
words.nonExample: An infection that keeps spreading through the body is not benign.

apps.academic: In biology, a benign growth stays in one place and does not invade other tissue.
apps.spoken: It looked scary, but it was a benign mistake and nothing broke.
apps.writing: Use benign to say that something is harmless or gently meant, in contrast to something threatening.

cloze.s: The test results were ___: the spot on the scan was harmless and needed only a yearly checkup.

cloze2.s: What looked like a threatening storm cloud was only a ___ patch of fog that burned off by noon.

misuse.s: The benign wolf growled and snapped at anyone who came near the den.
misuse.why: Benign means harmless or gentle; growling and snapping show a threat.

visual.alt: A stethoscope beside a green check mark.

words.frame: I knew it was benign when ___.

words.def: A desire to hurt or harm someone, often out of spite.
words.ex: The prank was not meant with malice; Jo only wanted to make the team laugh.
words.ex2: Her note was full of malice, listing every mistake Dan had made and mocking him for each one.
words.nonExample: An accidental bump in a crowded hallway carries no malice.

apps.academic: The law treats harm done with malice more seriously than harm done by accident.
apps.spoken: I said it without malice, but I can see why it stung.
apps.writing: Use malice for the intention to hurt, which separates a cruel act from an accident.

cloze.s: The rumor was spread out of ___, because the writer wanted her rival to feel embarrassed.

cloze2.s: He said he felt no ___ toward the winner, only disappointment that the race was over.

misuse.s: She acted with malice when she secretly baked a cake to cheer up her friend.
misuse.why: Malice is a wish to hurt; baking a cake to cheer someone up is the opposite.

visual.alt: An angry face with burst lines beside it.

words.frame: The act was done with malice because ___.

words.def: Meant to hurt, embarrass, or harm someone; full of ill will.
words.ex: Someone posted a malicious rumor about the new student to make her feel unwelcome.
words.ex2: The computer virus was malicious software designed to erase files and steal passwords.
words.nonExample: A joke that makes the person being teased laugh too is not malicious.

segs.m: full of; having the quality of

morph.note: The final e of malice is dropped before -ious.

apps.academic: Fact-checkers separate an honest mistake from a malicious falsehood spread to mislead.
apps.spoken: I don't think she was being malicious; she just didn't think.
apps.writing: Use malicious to describe an act or message that is meant to cause harm, not one that merely turns out badly.

cloze.s: The ___ comment was posted late at night to make the team captain look foolish in front of everyone.

cloze2.s: Police said the fire was not an accident but a ___ act committed by someone who wanted to cause damage.

misuse.s: The malicious gardener lovingly watered every plant and shared tomatoes with the neighbors.
misuse.why: Malicious means meant to harm; caring for plants and neighbors is the opposite.

visual.alt: A laptop with a harmful virus symbol on the screen.

words.frame: The message was malicious because it was meant to ___.

words.def: Wishing harm on others; showing a strong desire to do evil.
words.ex: The malevolent villain smiled as he planned how to ruin the festival.
words.ex2: A malevolent stare from across the room made Lia pull her coat tighter.
words.nonExample: A grumpy neighbor who only wants to be left alone is not malevolent.

morph.note: Male is the form of mal that appears before a vowel sound here.

apps.academic: In many stories, a malevolent character is defined by the harm he or she wishes on others, not only by the harm done.
apps.spoken: The way he smiled at the mess he made was almost malevolent.
apps.writing: Use malevolent for strong, deliberate ill will, as in a villain; use unkind for smaller matters.

cloze.s: The ___ queen in the fairy tale cast a spell on the village simply because she enjoyed its sorrow.

cloze2.s: A ___ whisper drifted from the dark hallway, and the children stopped, certain that someone wished them harm.

misuse.s: The malevolent nurse wished every patient a quick recovery and a happy life.
misuse.why: Malevolent means wishing harm; wishing patients well is the opposite.

visual.alt: A shadowy figure with glowing eyes under a dark moon.

words.def: A failure of a machine or system to work the way it should.
words.ex: A malfunction in the school's alarm system sent everyone outside on a cold morning.
words.ex2: The pilot calmly reported an engine malfunction and began the checklist for landing.
words.nonExample: A tool that works perfectly all day has had no malfunction.

apps.academic: Engineers study a malfunction to find out which part failed and how to prevent it next time.
apps.spoken: There was a malfunction with the projector, so we used the whiteboard.
apps.writing: Use malfunction for a machine or system that stops working properly; people make mistakes, machines malfunction.

cloze.s: A ___ in the vending machine caused it to drop three bags of chips instead of one.

cloze2.s: Engineers traced the blackout to a ___ in a single switch at the power station.

misuse.s: The scientist praised the robot's flawless performance and called the day's results a total malfunction.
misuse.why: A malfunction is a failure; flawless performance is the opposite.

visual.alt: A gear with a warning triangle over it.

words.def: Dangerous and likely to spread or grow worse, as a disease can; also, showing deep ill will.
words.ex: A malignant tumor can invade nearby tissue, so doctors treat it quickly.
words.ex2: Critics described the villain's malignant influence on the kingdom, which poisoned every friendship.
words.nonExample: A freckle that never changes is not malignant.

apps.academic: In medicine, a malignant growth can spread; in literature, a malignant influence spreads harm through a community.
apps.spoken: The doctor said it was not malignant, and the whole family breathed again.
apps.writing: Use malignant for harm that spreads or grows worse; use it carefully, because it is serious.

cloze.s: Because the growth was ___, the surgeon recommended removing it right away.

cloze2.s: The rumor became a ___ force in the school, spreading from hallway to hallway and poisoning friendships.

misuse.s: The malignant tumor was harmless and would never spread or change.
misuse.why: Malignant means dangerous and spreading; harmless and unchanging is benign.

passage.title: A Gift for Hollis Middle School
paras: Last spring, an anonymous benefactor offered to pay for a greenhouse at Hollis Middle School. The letter, signed only "a friend of this school," called the gift beneficial for science classes and for the whole neighborhood. Principal Vega read it aloud on Monday, and the hallways buzzed for days.

The first beneficiary was the seventh-grade science class, who planted tomatoes and herbs in raised beds. Their teacher, Mr. Okoye, called the donor benevolent, "a person who truly wishes the school well." Then a malfunction in the watering system left half the seedlings dry, and a quieter kind of trouble began.

Someone posted a rumor that Mr. Okoye himself was the donor and had taken the money from the lunch fund. The rumor was malicious, and everyone suspected malice rather than a mistake, because it appeared the same night a rival club lost a vote. A few students called it benign gossip. Mr. Okoye did not.

"A rumor is like a growth in the body," he told his class. "A benign growth stays where it is and does no harm. A malignant one spreads and damages everything near it. A rumor meant to hurt is malignant." Priya asked how anyone could stop it. "Ask for evidence," he said, "and refuse to pass it on."

By Friday, no one could find the source of the rumor, but it had stopped spreading. The school never learned the identity of its benefactor, though Ms. Vega was sure the donor would have been sad to see a gift meant to help the school stir up such a malevolent mood. Under the greenhouse's new sign, the class painted a single line: "Grow something good."

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "malice" most nearly means
choices: a mistake made in a hurry
a feeling of confusion
a wish to hurt someone
a silence that follows an argument
qs.why: Malice is a desire to harm; the passage says the rumor looked deliberate, not like an honest mistake.

qs.q: Why does Mr. Okoye compare a rumor to a growth in the body?
choices: He wants students to study biology instead of gossip.
He is explaining why the greenhouse plants died.
He thinks a harmful rumor can spread and hurt many people, as a dangerous growth can.
He believes every rumor is harmless if it stays small.
qs.why: He contrasts a benign growth, which stays put, with a malignant one, which spreads; he says a rumor meant to hurt is the second kind.

qs.q: Which detail from the passage best supports the idea that the donor was benevolent?
choices: The letter was signed only "a friend of this school."
The greenhouse was built in the spring.
Principal Vega read the letter on a Monday.
The seedlings were left dry for half a day.
qs.why: A gift offered without a name suggests the donor wanted to help, not to be praised.

qs.q: Why do a few students call the rumor "benign gossip"?
choices: They think it will not hurt anyone.
They think it is true.
They wrote the rumor themselves.
They believe Mr. Okoye should ignore the greenhouse.
qs.why: Benign means harmless; the students believe the gossip does no damage, and Mr. Okoye disagrees.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
choices: Donors should always be named in public.
Greenhouses are too expensive for middle schools.
Teachers should handle every rumor without help from students.
A good gift can be harmed by a rumor, but people can slow it by asking for evidence and not passing it on.
qs.why: The gift is a good thing, the rumor threatens it, and Mr. Okoye's advice is to ask for evidence and refuse to pass the rumor along.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words built on the roots bene (good, well) and mal (bad, badly), read a short narrative about a gift and a harmful rumor at a school, practice the endings -ent, -ous, and -ary, and write about kind and harmful acts. The unit's habit is to use roots to predict meaning and then check the prediction in context.

notes.va.beneficial.adj: Beneficial focuses on results: something helps. Show the root chain bene + fic + -ial and connect to benefit. Contrast with benevolent: beneficial describes the effect; benevolent describes the wish. Ask for a thing that is beneficial but not benevolent, such as sunshine.
notes.va.benevolent.adj: Benevolent is about the wish to do good (bene + vol, 'wish' + -ent). Draw the parallel with malevolent on a two-column chart. Students often use it for any kind person; prompt for the wish behind an action.
notes.va.beneficiary.n: A beneficiary receives; a benefactor gives. The two words are easy to swap, so use a simple diagram with an arrow from giver to receiver. The ending -ary appears as -iary after fic; point out the spelling shift.
notes.va.benefactor.n: Benefactor is a person who gives (bene + fact, 'do', + -or). Link to factory and fact as other uses of fact. Distinguish from beneficiary with an arrow diagram. Ask students to tell the story of one benefactor they know about in their community.
notes.va.benign.adj: Benign means harmless or gently meant. It begins with a form of the root bene, but the spelling is shortened, so students cannot decode it by parts alone. Pair with malignant in a science context and a story context so students see both uses.
notes.va.malice.n: Malice is the intention to hurt. Stress intention: a hurt caused by accident has no malice. Students may try to say 'maliced'; malice is a noun. Connect to malicious and malevolent in a ladder of ill will.
notes.va.malicious.adj: Malicious is malice + -ious (full of), with the e dropped. It describes acts and messages meant to harm. Use rumor and computer-virus examples. Clarify that a mistake that hurts is not malicious unless it was meant to hurt.
notes.va.malevolent.adj: Malevolent (male, 'bad' + vol, 'wish' + -ent) is the mirror image of benevolent. It is stronger than malicious because it describes a general wish for harm, often in villains. Ask students to find a malevolent and a malicious character in a book they know.
notes.va.malfunction.n: Malfunction is mal + function. Teach it as the easiest decoding win in the unit: students can see the parts. Machines malfunction; people make mistakes. Use real examples from school (a projector, a printer).
notes.va.malignant.adj: Malignant has two serious uses: a dangerous, spreading growth, and a deeply ill-willed influence. Keep medical talk factual and calm, and avoid asking students about their own family health. Contrast with benign and use the rumor metaphor in the passage.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see malevolent. I know mal means bad and vol means wish, so it might mean wishing harm. The sentence says the villain smiled as he planned to ruin a festival, which matches. Benevolent has bene and vol, so it should mean wishing good. The roots predicted the meaning, and the context confirmed it.'
discuss: Which word is stronger, malicious or malevolent, and what evidence from a story supports your answer?
Can someone be benevolent and make a mistake? What would you call the mistake?
misconceptions: Benefactor and beneficiary mean the same thing.
Benign always means kind; it often means only harmless.
A malfunction is a mistake a person makes.
Malice is any harm, even by accident.
extend: Make a root web for bene and mal using ten real words from dictionaries, and mark which ones you could predict by parts.
Write a short story with a benefactor, a beneficiary, and a malicious rumor, and have a partner underline each unit word.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Return to benevolent/malevolent and benign/malignant as paired opposites after two days and at one week. The unit 2 words partisan, manipulate, and allegiance return when students discuss why a rumor spreads or who benefits from it.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: beneficioso, benévolo, beneficiario, benefactor, benigno, mala intención (malice; malicia in Spanish can also mean cleverness or mischief), malicioso, malévolo, mal funcionamiento, maligno.
